cards.title: The Daily 3: Cut to Three Needle-Movers
cards.summary: Each day pick only the top 3 tasks that move the store forward and say no to the other 97%.
cards.use_when: Weekly planning for a lean ecommerce team or solo operator overwhelmed by merchandising, marketing, and ops tasks.
steps: Each morning (or the night before), list everything you could do across your store — product pages, ads, inventory, email, support.
Force-rank and select only 3 tasks that most move the needle (e.g. fix the top PDP, launch the restock email, resolve a checkout drop-off).
Work top to bottom through those 3 before touching anything else.
Say no to the other 97% deliberately; defer, delegate, or delete them.
Review the pattern over weeks so recurring 'yes' items reflect your real priorities, not noise.
caveats: Source is the presenter's personal operating rule, not a proven system for all teams.
Some urgent ops issues (stockouts, payment failures) may need same-day handling outside the 3.

cards.title: "Audience Comes Last": Build to Your Taste, Not Market Guessing
cards.summary: Ignore surveys and focus groups during the creative act; rely on personal intuition and taste, then test in market.
cards.use_when: Designing brand identity, packaging, creative direction, or new products where you're tempted to poll customers first.
steps: Separate the creation phase from the validation phase: block the audience out while conceiving the brand, product, or creative.
Lean on your own taste, intuition, and judgment as the core input rather than surveys or focus groups (the Rick Rubin / Steve Jobs principle the presenter cites).
Trust the signal from your inner voice to distill to one simple idea.
After creating, take it to market where real behavior (clicks, add-to-cart, repeat orders) is the test.
Note the source's framing: the audience only knows what has come before, so customers tend to ask for a faster horse rather than something genuinely new.
caveats: This concerns the creative act; it is not a license to skip customer research, pricing tests, or post-launch data.
The presenter attributes this to Rubin and Jobs — treat as their philosophy, not a validated universal method.

cards.title: Let Weirdness Become the Brand's Authentic Edge
cards.summary: Digging into your own quirks and 'woo woo' interests produces authentic differentiation competitors don't copy.
cards.use_when: Positioning a store in a crowded category where every brand sounds and looks the same.
steps: Identify the beliefs, niche interests, or approaches you hold that others in your category call odd or dismiss.
Ignore critics who say it's too niche or nobody cares; the source kept his 'soulful' angle despite pushback.
Lean that unfair advantage into brand voice, product curation, and creative instead of flattening to category norms.
Use the search through your own weirdness to find what is genuinely you — the presenter says authenticity comes from that exploration.
Express it consistently across PDP copy, packaging, and social so it reads as a coherent brand, not a gimmick.
caveats: Distinctiveness can narrow appeal; ensure the core offer still solves a clear customer problem.
Authenticity claims are the presenter's philosophy, not a measured conversion driver.
cards.source_name: the psychology of building a brand everyone loves.docx

cards.title: Obsess Over the Craft, Not the Metrics
cards.summary: Betting maximum effort on the craft every time compounds exponentially, and obsession becomes contagious to an audience.
cards.use_when: Allocating effort between chasing metrics (views, follower counts) versus improving the actual product, photos, or content quality.
steps: Redirect effort from metric-chasing to mastering the craft: cinematography, lighting, copy, product quality.
Go all-in on each project rather than spreading thin — the source cites Mr. Beast 'betting the farm' each video.
Aim to solve the problem three times deeper than competitors; different solutions follow from deeper work.
Pick a single format on a single platform and try to make it best-in-world rather than dabbling across all of them (the presenter says dabbling gets lost in the noise).
Example cited: hand-drawing concept images on LinkedIn out of genuine obsession led to ~110,000 followers in a month — treat this as an anecdote, not a target.
caveats: Obsession compounding is the presenter's analogy, not a linear formula with verified numbers.
The Mr. Beast and LinkedIn follower results are case examples, not promises.
cards.source_name: the psychology of building a brand everyone loves.docx

cards.title: Insanely Simple: Strip to One Idea
cards.summary: Relentlessly simplify products, UX, and messaging to one clear thing, on the Henry Ford principle that people don't know what they want.
cards.use_when: Simplifying a cluttered PDP, navigation, product line, or ad concept that has too many competing messages.
steps: Iterate toward fewer elements: the source recounts iPhone prototypes going from three buttons to one to a buttonless interface under Jobs.
Apply the same to messaging — Apple's ads made a simple, memorable comparison rather than an exhaustive feature list.
Distill your product or store down to one simple thing customers can remember.
Cut feature creep and competing CTAs; each extra element dilutes the signal.
Note the Ford framing: customers didn't ask for a car, they asked for a faster horse — so simplicity often means leading, not polling.
caveats: Simplification can strip genuinely useful features; test whether customers still complete the task.
The Apple/Jobs story is illustrative, not a documented playbook you can copy directly.
cards.source_name: the psychology of building a brand everyone loves.docx

cards.title: Choose One Format on One Platform
cards.summary: Dabbling across platforms gets lost in the noise; obsessing over a single format on a single platform sets you apart.
cards.use_when: Deciding which organic channel to build for a store instead of posting thinly across X, LinkedIn, YouTube, and Instagram.
steps: Pick one platform and one format (e.g. a weekly founder video, a daily concept image, one recurring email).
Commit to making that single format the best in the world rather than spreading effort.
Refuse to treat it as a side hobby or something to dabble in — the presenter says that path gets lost in the noise.
Obsess over the format's craft, not the follower count.
Let the format compound: the source's hand-drawn concept images shared thousands of times and grew LinkedIn by ~110k in a month (an anecdote, not a benchmark).
caveats: Single-platform focus trades reach for depth; revisit the choice only after sufficient reps.
The follower-growth example is a case result, not a repeatable promise.

cards.title: Go Deep, Not Wide: Shape the Company's Character
cards.summary: Iconic brands go deep rather than wide, and deliberately training through 'pain and suffering' refines a company's character.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to broaden a product line or deepen an existing category and internal standard of quality.
steps: Bias toward depth: improve the core product, sourcing, or experience rather than adding categories.
Adopt the source's framing of using 'pain and suffering' deliberately — i.e. embrace hard refinements that train the character of the company.
Treat the goal as building an icon over decades, not chasing the next product launch.
Apply the principle to team standards: obsess over craft quality so the brand's depth shows in every touchpoint.
Remember the closing line: icons aren't born, they're built.
caveats: Depth can mean slower diversification; weigh against the realities of your category and cash flow.
The 'pain and suffering' language is the presenter's rhetorical framing, not an operating metric.
